412.t: Progress, the new thing and no regrets
412.s: Hodes questions whether the new is better and says he was fortunate to play that music. DeMichael says he followed his heart.
412.q: No, everything is -- and for that reason, we have lost something. We've lost this tremendous training that these people had and they became what they are. And it's not that these people today -- I'm not faulting them, I'm faulting the conditions. And you say, in summing up, would you do it over…

412.t: Closing words: the moment in music is priceless
412.s: In closing Hodes tells of a pianist who saved and lost everything. He says music is priceless and he regrets nothing.
412.q: -- may I say this in closing? I met a pianist who worked during the same years that I did, in bars and clubs. And he read the specs and he played the floor show, and he saved his money and he lost his eyesight and he lost all his money in the Crash.

412.t: If he had to do it again
412.s: Asked to sum up, Hodes says he stayed out of big bands and would take the same path. He regrets missing Joe Oliver.
412.q: I'm not going to say I'd do it all over you, like the joke. No, if I had to do it all over again, I'd consider myself one of the most fortunate people in the world that the direction that I took, that I stayed out of big bands, where I would have been -- I could learn how to play in big bands, it's…

953.t: How he feels about interviews and changing views
953.s: Interviews are part of his job, and he says his views are changing as he becomes more enlightened.
953.q: Well, you see, what’s happening with me, Larry, is that...all of these questions are sort of...that question does–it’s sort of changing now, because I’m getting more enlightened, now. I’m, I’m advancing in age, so hopefully that’s a good sign. I know I’m not going to have five, or 100, more years…

953.s: Success is material comfort in a small way, but what matters is being a better person; he is 80 and will continue.
953.q: Well [chuckling]...success, wow. Well, I hate to think in the terms of uh the world we live in, the material world we live in, but uh it’s successful when I can uh...I feel that success is uh...uh being able to uh...take a town-car instead of having to uh take the train. Being able to do things of…

172.t: Being one of the few old musicians left
172.s: Ridgley says leaving the saxophone was best and he is content.
172.q: I made a pretty good... I got along pretty good by being in the saxophone. I think I made the best move. You see? I've made all those old fellas who are gone.

390.t: Closing reflections and an early New Orleans record
390.s: Desvigne calls music the greatest part of his life, mentions little money, and recalls an early record made in New Orleans before the tape ends.
390.q: But I remember all those things, you know. all those things you know but I think it was the greatest part of my life playing music all that many years. Yes that's something you never did. Yeah of course we didn't make any money we didn't have a chance to make any money in those days you know. Well…

43.s: She enjoyed big audiences and says she made the most money at the Nest Club.
43.q: Well, I tell ya, I enjoyed singing on, being to the public, you know, bigger the crowd, but then I, you know, see? I enjoyed that. That thing impressed me whenever we, I walked out with a bed, it was a big audience and something like that. Is that what you mean? Yeah.

128.s: The men say they have no regrets and would play until they cannot.
128.q: You had to go back to music again, start a new life.

392.t: Memories of the bands, Sweet Emma, and closing
392.s: Happy memories of Lewis, Celestin and Robichaux, bringing Sweet Emma back, and wrapping up.
392.ch: Later years and the club's fate
392.q: No, it's a difficult thing, I mean, what you'd like to have and what you can afford, I guess, to see, uh, whether it's, uh, trying to run a nightclub with entertainment or, uh, buying an automobile, I guess you've got to do what you can afford to do. Of course, we tried, we tried, and we, uh, we…

303.t: Rex proclamation, scrapbook reflections and recent work
303.s: Riddick shows a Rex 1967 proclamation, a recording with Johnny Wiggs, and says the scrapbook's satisfaction is having been there; he still wants to work.
303.q: On a proclamation. Rex King of Carnival. This was given to me, you know, playing on Rex bandwagon. Rex 1967. Uh huh. Sure with Manjapanie. Sure with Manjapanie. Had the band. 된 stuff... 된 stuff... 된 stuff... 된 stuff...

767.t: The thrill of hearing himself on a jukebox
767.s: Harris says the pay was small, but hearing himself on a jukebox was a thrill.
767.ch: Boots and His Buddies and Wild Cherry
767.q: But I mean playing it, that was a kick. That was a thousand dollars right back. Sure. Guys would ask me, how does it feel to walk up and drop a liquor in a jukebox and hear yourself play? I said oh man, there's nothing to it but hell I was thrilling inside you know. It was thrilling inside.

535.s: He has no regret about when he was born and agrees the good old days are now.
535.q: I never felt that way. Yeah I don’t regret not being around during the heyday of what they — and some people say man don’t worry about — there was never a heyday. But I don’t regret being born when I was born.

397.t: Being a lucky man whose dreams came true
397.s: Berroa reflects on how few immigrant musicians see their dreams fulfilled; Rowe shares his own college dreams.
397.q: Well yeah. Thanks. I can see that I’m a lucky man. I’m a lucky man because not everybody comes to the United States and fulfills their dreams. Speaking about music you know a lot of musicians from different countries come to the United States with an idea, with a dream and not everybody has been…

979.t: Which era she would live in
979.s: She would not trade the present for another time, though Michelangelo's era appeals.
979.q: I don’t know, maybe the time Michelangelo and the time these people that did many, many things at one time, and they also lived long, some of them lived long lives and they had a chance to really get into a lot of different fields and things. Maybe. I don’t know. I like it now.

746.t: Being a woman in creative music; a wonderful life
746.s: She never felt disadvantaged by gender in her milieu, though sometimes overlooked by festivals, and calls her life a dream.
746.q: I never did feel that. I never did feel that because of the milieu that I was in. It was really about the music and who could play the music. You know? There was never a thought of is it a woman or a man, whatever, at least to my knowledge there mostly wasn’t. You know? Sometimes when it would come…

720.t: Reflecting on a career of writing music
720.s: He feels blessed to write for a living, from a one-musician town.
720.q: Yeah it’s always going to be there, but a lot of those people are gone. It’s probably never going to be performed again but I really feel blessed in being able to do that for a living. How much better does it get? I sit there at my piano thinking this is what I do for a living.

580.t: Whether he wishes he'd lived in another era
580.s: Israels has never thought about it and feels lucky to have had his career when he did.
580.q: I never thought about it. I haven’t thought about that. Huh. My mother used to say, “What if there were no hypothetical questions?” Think about that.

521.t: Working for love and her cable access award
521.s: She congratulated on her PACE award, she says she learned from Alfred to love work, and reflects on the arts.
521.q: I do. I learned that. I always enjoyed working. But I learned it from him because he was so in love with his work. In fact on his gravestone I had printed “Through jazz he lived the life he loved.” And I learned that from him. You don’t always feel like working. But if you love that work you’ll go…

416.t: Final reflections on the greatest era
416.s: He says he played with the greatest musicians in the greatest era of American music and is glad he was part of it.
416.q: In fact I played, my final saying, I played with the greatest musicians in the world, I think, the greatest. All the best. And I did come up in the greatest era of music the United States ever had. And I’m glad I was part of it you know. It was the greatest era I think. If you remember that era.

790.t: Moved to tears by playing New Orleans music
790.s: Overwhelmed by yesterday's performance and the richness of his life in music.
790.q: Right. Hey what are you doing here? You get in the truck too. You never know. But New Orleans has been great for me personally. My life and my life experiences, like a tear up and I well up when I think about it, like yesterday performing, I was telling my wife, you know, I always forget to bring a…

459.s: Sauter-Finegan would be the part of life to sustain; wishes his wife were present.
459.q: Because she’d grin a mile wide hearing me talk like this. And we were both so proud of our daughter Krissy. We’ve been blessed.

85.t: His place in history, regrets and what he enjoyed
85.s: Carter wants only to be remembered as having been here, would change some missed opportunities, and enjoyed it all.
85.q: No, all I would like to remember for is having been here. Whatever contribution I may have made, if any, is to be made by others, not by me . . . to be recognized by others, not by me. I don’t know that I’ve made any real contribution. I’ve done what I set out to do, and that was have fun with the…

703.s: He reflects on his good life, fishing, gardening and family.
703.q: I count my blessings. I’m very lucky. I’ve very lucky to be able to sit here with you guys right here, with Rosemary, with our family and our children, to be able to sit here in this house. Think of all – to be able to have the health to be able to talk about the things that we’ve been talking…

491.t: Music keeps him young; loving the work, the film years and returning to jazz
491.s: Golson speaks of the privilege of earning a living from music, contrasts it with truck driving and film scoring, and says he returned to his first love.
491.q: Yeah, of a sort, of course, because I look forward to it every day, just like breathing. Yeah, I do. Although I don’t know how to do – somebody told me once, when I said, “I don’t know how to do anything else” – he said, “You can dig ditches.” I said, “Yeah, you’re right, but I’d rather think the…

507.t: Recording break and how his careers flow together
507.s: After an interruption, Schwartz and Schuller marvel at how his careers connect.
507.q: Can you imagine how fascinating my life is? It’s unbelievable, how lucky I am.

224.t: Not wanting to relive the past in an interview
224.s: Haynes says going back over difficult times irritates him once he has dealt with them.
224.q: No, because then you started getting into laying out and you made me think – you see, that’s what I mean about – you start re-living certain things over again as you talk about them. Then sometimes it’s something that you don’t want to re-live over again. You know what I mean? So that’s why I said,…

108.t: No regrets: his parents' divorce and Clark Terry
108.s: Wilder says he regrets little, tells how he forgave his father, and compares himself to Terry.
108.q: Sometimes there are some things that I say, maybe I wish I had had more opportunities to play classical music, or something like that, but then, at the same time, when I look at it, I say to myself, but I’ve been fortunate. I’ve been blessed as it is. So I don’t complain about it. It’s just like –…

227.s: Mandel closes by saying he is proud to be part of the American songwriting tradition and lucky to have spent his life doing what he loves.
227.q: Boy, it’s wonderful just to be among all that and to be able to – we have such great literature to – you know this is the great treasury of American art, is the songwriting that has come out of this century of American music. And I’m just very proud to even however remotely, be associated with it.

80.t: No regrets: proud to have made it as a musician
80.s: Looking back he would change nothing and is proudest that he became the musician he decided to be at age four.
80.q: Well, I'm trying to think. What am I proudest of? They asked me, when I was a very small kid, three or four years old, four years old, not three. I do remember, four years old. I knew I wanted to be a musician, because I had heard the music, and I saw my brother and my dad playing, and they tried…

229.t: No regrets about a musician's life
229.s: Asked if he would do anything differently, Blakeney says he is satisfied and was paid to see the world.
229.ch: Film work, recording and looking back
229.q: I think I'm satisfied with it; I don't think I'd go back and do it any different because the experience I received, it was a wonderful experience. I couldn't have had it any other way.

614.t: Would he do it all again? The music is worth it
614.s: Herman says he would do it all over, because of the music, stimulation, people and travel.
614.ch: Looking back, big bands and sidemen
614.q: Well, I've never really tried to make an evaluation, but I do honestly believe that if I had to do it all over again, I would. And I'd probably do it pretty much the same way, and plod through it somehow, as I have.

66.s: She would live it again, one-nighters and starvation included, and the interview closes.
66.q: Beautiful. I'd live it again, go over the same things, one-nighters with Andy Kirk, starvation, and many, many things that happened. I'd go over it again.

146.t: Wishing he had stayed an electrician
146.s: Smith says he wishes he had stayed with electrical work in the 1920s and become a contractor.
146.ch: Looking back and the New York years
146.q: No. That was back in the 20's, before I started playing music for a living. And I wish many days I had stayed with it, because I'd have stayed home here, and today I might have had something.

98.t: No regrets staying in Chicago; the 50th anniversary
98.s: Saunders has no regret not joining big bands; community support is selling tickets for his fiftieth anniversary.
98.ch: Chicago pioneers, community and New Orleans brotherhood
98.q: Well, see, that was the way my life was all the way through. And this is why it's been such a pleasure. Somebody asked me about Chicago, I says, did I regret it, not going with the different big bands and things like that. I said, no, I don't regret it. I said, I've lived a beautiful life right…
